The idea of the 2027 Velo Field Test is to look at today’s gravel bikes and try to identify the direction things are going, to figure out what the future of gravel looks like. Our choice for this is the Factor Sarana, and I personally could not be happier.

The Factor Sarana is designed to be an ultra-endurance race bike. It’s a category of bike that some people say isn’t real, yet it was the winning bike for this year’s Tour Divide race. It was also, realistically speaking, a bike designed with Factor athlete Rob Britton in mind. That seems like a real category of racing to me, and it’s also a category that actually applies very well to many other types of racing and everyday riders. Perhaps call it endurance gravel if that makes more sense to you.

The bike you’d want for ultra-endurance racing is, in many ways, an all-around bike. It’s not so aggressive that you can’t hold the position for days of racing. It’s a bike that helps you when you can barely think straight, and it won’t punish you if you get distracted. A good ultra-endurance bike is also a bike that keeps you comfortable over long distances.

If you are thinking that maybe a bike with those qualities sounds pretty good for you, you aren’t alone. Comfortable, predictable, and capable are perfect traits for most people riding bikes, and that’s why we felt like the Sarana was a good candidate for the future direction of gravel riding. I happen to be thrilled because ultra-endurance is my passion, so if that’s the direction we are going, great. Let’s talk about what I like, and what I don’t, about the Factor Sarana.

I have to admit that one of the things I love about the Sarana is that it’s targeting a part of the market that I really enjoy. Never mind that this is a gravel bike for a moment; think in terms of road bikes. Inherently, this is an endurance bike, and endurance bikes tend to lack appeal. People are not drawn to the sensible bike, so on the road side, it becomes an “all-road” bike—despite really not being that in many cases. What does a brand do on the gravel side? You can’t sprinkle in some gravel marketing; it’s already a gravel bike. The solution seems to have been to focus on ultra-endurance as a way to jazz this up.

That’s the most cynical way to view it, though. Instead, think about what ultra-endurance actually demands and how that translates to a bike. It also happens to align with Factor athletes, and that makes it authentic.

To bring this to a point: what I like about the Factor Sarana is the leaf-spring rear triangle design. What I’m talking about is a system that we’ve seen other brands take various passes at, but Factor is a company that takes pride in carbon engineering. Rather than employ a mechanical hinge like Cannondale, Factor started by dropping the chainstays near the bottom bracket. This design allows for the necessary space of 57mm tire clearance with a 425mm chainstay, but it also creates a curve that arcs gracefully up before finally curving down at the rear axle. Then, right at the top of that apex, where the design puts the most leverage on the chainstay, it’s intentionally flattened and thinned.

This chainstay design is also paired with a curved seat tube that has deeply dropped seatstays. That provides a designated flex point in the seat tube, with the seatstay positioned exactly where it needs to be to push on it and drive that movement.

This shaping results in a lot of movement in the rear triangle, but it requires nothing from the end user. By utilizing geometry and carbon layup, Factor created a frame that flexes vertically to absorb impacts while remaining laterally stiff for power transfer. You get a bit of suspension without needing to deal with the weight and maintenance of a mechanical system. Factor claims this provides an “18% reduction in vibration amplitude,” and Factor has also thrown a figure of 10mm of travel at me. Either way, the exact math doesn’t matter because the result is that you can feel it, and it’s just there without drawbacks.

This also plays perfectly with the 57mm of tire clearance. Bigger tires mean more suspension and more capability. Combine that with the vertical movement of the rear triangle, and you have this great combination of comfort and capability without dealing with the bobbing or maintenance of a shock system.

Weight. This bike is heavy. We tested the suspension version, and ready to ride (minus pedals), it came in at 9.58 kg (21.1 lbs). Of course, a large part of what some of the team appreciated while testing in Squamish was that front suspension. My personal take is that while the RockShox fork felt great when out of the saddle, I’d prefer the bike without it. Unfortunately, ditching the fork doesn’t fully solve the issue.

Even if you take that suspension away, it’s still a ~1,200g frame. In fact, we can do a bit of math: the rigid fork is 550 grams according to Factor, and the suspension fork is roughly 1,260 grams. In theory, swapping those out leaves you with an 8.87 kg (19.55 lb) bike built with SRAM Force—and saddled with a premium price tag.

To put that in perspective, the version we tested came in heavier than the 32-inch, metal-framed Salsa Fargo, and nearly matches the Pivot Les SL drop-bar mountain bike. Of course, our Field Test was designed to include wildly different bikes, so if we instead look at the Cannondale Topstone Carbon 1 AXS Lefty as a more direct comparison, the Sarana is slightly lighter at 9.58 kg versus 9.8 kg. However, the Cannondale is also $2,000 less and comes with SRAM Rival instead of Force.…

Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

The 2026 gravel season has come and gone, and I, for one, am tired. Since March, I have been on the gravel beat for Velo, covering all the tech and racing from the biggest gravel races in the United States.

It all started for me close to home at BWR Arizona and stretched out through the spring, summer, and early fall to Big Sugar Gravel in Bentonville just a few days ago.

While all this travel, writing, videos, and riding adds up—it’s also been a lot of fun. I have had a blast checking in with many of the riders, showcasing all of the new major gravel bike releases, and even jumping in the racing action a few times myself.

At the end of the year, it’s clear that while gravel might not be growing at the same rate it was a few years ago, it’s still the playground of fun innovation and tech that keeps me and so many others coming back. The pro side of things especially continues to be interesting. In gravel racing, the pursuit of top-end speed has proved to trickle down throughout the industry since gravel speed increasingly equals gravel comfort.

To celebrate the season that was, and to survey where the discipline is after a half-decade of professional racing in the Life Time Grand Prix, here are my big takeaways from gravel tech in 2026:

No matter how much some people argue, the cat is out of the bag: we are not going back to small gravel tires. Even on terrain with plenty of smooth tarmac, if there is enough dirt on a route to justify more than 40mm tires, the technology around tires has improved to where 50s are almost always faster.

There are a few outliers—Cobe Freeburn, for instance, has run 45s a few times this year, including his gravel nationals win on the Trek Domane—but largely it is now a choice between 50 and 55mm treads.

For general riders, this is a really good thing. The falsehood that narrower gravel tires were faster held gravel back from having more comfortable setups. This new “bigger is better” mentality just makes sense across the board, and I can’t see 45s coming back.

Last year, suspension had a moment. Throughout the year, gravel suspension seemed to be making a move to take over the gravel racing tech.

From a large portion of the pro peloton sporting the forks at BWR AZ, the first race of the year, to some notable testing that said suspension with narrower tires might be faster, gravel suspension seemed to be building momentum.

That didn’t continue this year. Overwhelmingly, racers cut back on how much they used suspension forks. At technical races like BWR AZ, there still were a few suspension forks, including Russell Finsterwald’s winning bike, but at events like the Traka and Unbound it was all rigid bikes and big tires.

I still find there to be a great use case for suspension on gravel bikes, even with this pivot from racers. It can effectively bridge the gap between cross-country mountain bikes and race gravel bikes. Yet, tires have gotten better, and weight still matters in racing. Looking forward, gravel suspension forks likely will remain a small niche within the landscape of gravel race bikes.

Even in the face of big gravel tires, there remains a push and pull in theories around gravel bike geometry.

For some, the goal is length, stability, and creating bikes meant to handle the 50-55mm tires of modern gravel in a way that resembles the tougher terrain gravel includes. Others are dead set on trying their very best to keep making road bikes that can hold 2.2-inch tires.

Personally, I find one of these geometries much more compelling than the other one, but many disagree with me. There remains a split, even among some of the biggest bike brands, of what is best. Ultimately, that could lead to some people having the “wrong” bike. But until then, there is more variety in ride experience than ever.

Speaking of ride experience, the last and perhaps most important gravel tech development in 2026 has been 32-inch gravel bikes. While this is not the year they have taken over, Cam Jones riding a prototype 32-inch Scott Addict Gravel—in the same year that Scott released a new 29-inch gravel bike—shows just how much attention the budding wheel size has commanded.

That will not stop next year. From sources inside the industry, Trek, Scott, and Specialized are among a large number of companies that plan to unveil 32-inch gravel bikes next year.

At this point, we don’t know when, nor do we know what will be available to buy. Nevertheless, what I can say is this is the last year when major releases won’t include 32-inch bikes. Over the next year, the whole landscape will change, even if there will still be 29 options.

While all of this is speculative, it has been hanging over the gravel tech landscape this year almost as if it’s an impending attack from the Boogeyman. Personally, I just find it all very exciting, especially as I learn firsthand just how powerful a tool these new wheels are to ride.

Thanks for reading and, most of all, thanks for following our coverage from this year’s gravel racing season! We will be back for more in 2027. Yet, before that, let us know what you thought was the biggest gravel tech change in 2026 and what you predict will change in 2027.

In the search for what the future of gravel bikes will look like, one obvious direction is to take the concept all the way to mountain bikes. Half the comments already claim that modern gravel bikes are just mountain bikes anyway, so why not embrace the concept? The Pivot LES SL Drop Bar belongs to exactly this class of bike. The bike is a hardtail mountain bike with drop bars.

Pivot is not unique in offering something like this, and in the past, I’ve been somewhat of a critic of the idea. It’s easy to say this kind of bike is just a parts-bin grab. A brand has a bunch of unsold mountain bike frames, so what if someone looking at the numbers just sources a cockpit that will work? Now you’ve got a whole new category of riders to potentially sell a bike to, and investment is minimal.

If you follow that line of thinking, then you also realize the result will be a compromise. The Pivot LES SL is a lightweight carbon hardtail, and it wasn’t designed for drop-bar duties. The rear end uses boost spacing, so cranks and wheels designed for gravel bikes don’t fit. Good luck finding aero-focused wheels, and the bars that are specced are massively wide compared to shoulder sizes. Now that I’ve spent time with the bike, though, is that fair? Let’s get into my revised way of looking at a bike like this.

The best thing, and the worst thing, about this bike is the 100mm front suspension. In a way, I hate it, because unlike gravel suspension that often works as a set-and-forget kind of thing, the 100mm Fox front fork requires some recalibration. If you are used to something like the RockShox Rudy front suspension, this fork might bug you because it moves a lot. If you stand to sprint, good luck. It becomes a bobbing energy suck, and you are going to want to make liberal use of the lockout and adjustment knob. You will probably also want to adopt a much more mountain-bike-style riding stance, where standing to pedal is rare and you keep your weight back.

Despite all of that, this feature is what I like about the bike because it is, in large part, the entire point. If you prefer the feel and capabilities of a 30mm or 40mm front suspension fork, then this isn’t the bike for you. If you instead need the capabilities of an actual mountain bike, then you want that full 100mm of suspension goodness, and that’s worth putting up with the compromises. It feels like you can roll over anything that comes ahead of you, and this much suspension means better traction when you do it.

This fork is also what you want if you plan to spend days or weeks traveling across seriously rough terrain. Not the kind of terrain that a short-travel gravel fork can handle, but rough, rooted, and rocky singletrack across a country. You are going to be seated while pedaling, and as you roll over things, your hands and arms don’t have to be in a constant state of tension.

Now that I, as the resident roadie in our gravel bike Field Test, got to spend time with a bike in this category, I could also make the argument that this is what you want as a road-leaning rider. If you feel unsure of yourself when things get truly rough, then big suspension (for a drop-bar bike) is what will make the difference between always feeling unsure and really starting to feel capable. Just make sure you don’t expect to do too much mixed-surface riding, because that is not the happy place for this suspension or bike.

Although I mentioned some of the drawbacks of the 100mm suspension, I don’t really think that stuff is a big deal. You want that suspension because you want the traction. What actually does bother me is the lack of saddle-to-bar drop. It’s inherent to any 100mm suspension and fixing it is tricky, but if I could wave my wand and fix something, it would be this.

The reason it bugs me is that I want a bike that feels fast. When I really want to push hard, I am used to tucking in, getting aero, and just pedaling. In the case of the Pivot Les SL, it feels impossible to match that feeling because it’s so upright and the bars are super wide. Sure, I could swap the bars, but getting that long and low feeling is a bit more tricky.

The reason the problem exists is that 100mm of travel requires more space. The axle-to-crown length on a fork with this much travel pushes the front end up higher than a standard rigid gravel bike. While Pivot keeps the head tube as short as possible to compensate, you are still left with very little saddle-to-bar drop. Unless you are willing to swap in a radically negative-angled stem to slam the bars, you are going to be sitting relatively upright. It is a necessary compromise to fit that much suspension on a frame, but the result is a bike that feels incredibly capable in the rough, but somewhat sluggish and blocky when you are just trying to put your head down and crush a smooth fire road. This detail is why you sometimes see drop-bar conversions with bonkers-looking negative stems.

Unlike the 100mm suspension fork, I don’t believe this upright posture is really the point of the bike. While it is true that an upright position adds stability, if the bar and stem managed to get the racy position I like and I could combine that with the 100mm of travel, this bike would feel a whole lot different. It would shift the use case a little more toward gravel roads, but I would personally have a lot more fun riding it.…

Our quest to find the future of gravel bikes at the Velo Field Test has taken us on a long journey. We’ve test ridden six bikes that couldn’t be more different on a first impressions loop , and put the bikes through a series of head to head challenges . Now it’s time to test these bikes in the way that really matters: a big ride. In this final episode, we’re riding 100 kilometers (62 miles) up British Columbia’s Sea to Sky corridor from Squamish to Whistler.

In a discipline where people regularly ride hundreds of kilometers in one go, 100 isn’t the most insane distance. But it’s what’s contained in that distance that’s the challenge. Mike Levy has wracked the depths of his local knowledge to devise a course that hits all sorts of gravel terrain, and will push Josh and Logan to their limits as they in turn find the limits of the bikes.

There’s champagne gravel, gravel that is more aptly described as large rocks, steep climbs, technical single track, and some connectors on paved roads for good measure. Each of our six test bikes gets a chance to shine, and will also have its weaknesses glaringly exposed.

We have three riders and six bikes, so in order to test every bike on the ride, each tester will be switching out bikes at the halfway point. Who gets to pick what? Well we settled that in the most obvious way possible: go-karts. We found out that while Logan has Josh beat in a gravel race, Josh’s background hanging around L.A.’s underground street racing scene gave him the upper hand with track times. And that means he gets to pick what bikes Logan rides.

After hundreds of kilometers of riding and a series of head-to-head challenges, Levy, Josh, and Logan sit down to debate what the future of gravel bikes really looks like. Are bigger wheels the answer? Does suspension belong on gravel bikes? Are we sacrificing too much capability in the pursuit of speed? And most importantly, which of these six bikes would each tester actually take home?

The all-rounder: race it or go adventuring.

To settle the debate about the future of gravel once and for all (or perhaps muddy it more than ever), we’ve assembled three test riders who, like the bikes, couldn’t be more different.

Reformed mountain biker turned drop-bar obsessive Mike Levy leads the charge, bringing a technical, rowdy background and a preference for chunkier roads and adventuring far off the beaten path—on Earth and beyond.

He’s joined by Velo’s in-house team of tech editors. Josh Ross likes to ride long distances as efficiently as possible—catch him pedaling all day and night across the gravel roads of the Pacific Northwest and beyond. He’s all about pushing his personal boundaries, and finding the equipment that will help him go the extra mile (or extra 200 miles).

Having once finished 18th overall at the Unbound 200, Logan Jones-Wilkins can’t stop thinking about going fast and squeezing every drop of performance from gravel gear. But when he’s not mixing it up in the pointy end of races, he likes his gravel bike to be a medium for adventuring into the unknown.

That’s three different approaches to gravel, and, naturally, their takes are as varied as the riders themselves. Can they settle their differences and agree on anything? We may have to resort to some good ol’ fashioned tactics to resolve things—which may or may not mean go-kart racing.

To put these bikes to the ultimate test (and the riders too), we’ve taken everyone to the outdoor playground that is Squamish, British Columbia. Finding out the future of gravel means pushing bikes to their limits, so we’ve found a mix of terrain from single track to washboard fire roads to do just that.

We’re stress testing the bikes to get the most possible out of them. In this first episode, we’ve put together a test loop that takes our riders on a smattering of every kind of terrain one might consider gravel, from champagne roads, to loamy dirt trails, to slightly technical, rocky single track, and we’ve got climbing and descending for all of the above.

To keep our testing focused on the bikes themselves, we’ve brought in control tires, 50mm Schwalbe G-One RX tires run at the same tire pressure, mounted to Easton EC90 ALX wheels .

Velo Field Test wouldn’t happen without the support of these sponsors. A big thank you to Endura for providing kits and helmets, Schwalbe for tires, and Easton for wheels!

A special thank you to the crew who made this Velo Field Test a reality!

There’s more to come from the Velo Gravel Bike Field Test! We argue in depth about the future of gravel bikes on our podcast roundtable discussion, plus we have individual reviews for every single bike on test.

Life Time has unveiled standardized qualifying criteria for riders looking to enter the pro category at Unbound Gravel, Leadville, and its other marquee races.

For 2027, riders wishing to race in the pro fields will need to obtain an “LT Pro Number”. Some riders will qualify automatically based on their previous results in Life Time events. Others will need to submit an application with proof that they meet other standards, listed below.

Riders only need to qualify once per season and are good to go for the remaining races in the calendar year once they qualify. Receiving an LT Pro Number is not a race entry or guarantee of a spot at a race; it only allows a rider to enter the pro race. Riders still need to sign up for each race. It is also not an entry into the Life Time Grand Prix; rather, it allows racers to enter the pro field at those events.

An LT Pro number will be needed to enter the pro field in the seven races that also comprise the Life Time Grand Prix. The Sea Otter Classic Gravel Pro Race, Unbound Gravel 200, Leadville Trail 100 MTB, Chequamegon MTB Festival, Little Sugar MTB, Big Sugar Gravel, and The Rad Dirt Fest all require an LT Pro number for the pro race.

The announcement is Life Time’s latest change aimed at creating more standardized, transparent pro racing qualification. Life Time announced this summer standardized qualification criteria for making the 25-rider fields for the Life Time Grand Prix , the premier offroad racing series in North America.

As gravel racing has become more competitive and faster over the years, Life Time has taken steps in the name of safety, including moving the pros to their own start times ahead of the mass participation rides. Now, Life Time is hoping that standardized criteria will make the pro races safer by limiting spots to top riders.

“We love that our events bring together athletes of all ages and abilities, and create opportunities for people to challenge themselves,” said Michelle Duffy, director of the Life Time Grand Prix. “At the same time, mass participant events like Unbound and Leadville are fast and can be tightly packed, particularly at the front of the field. Establishing clear, performance-based criteria for the Pro start helps ensure riders competing at the front have demonstrated the experience and ability to race safely at that level, while providing a transparent pathway for athletes to earn their place.”

Being fast doesn’t necessarily go hand in hand with being a safe racer, but the new criteria should help limit the pro fields to more experienced riders.

There are a number of pathways to qualify for Pro status at Life Time races.

Several criteria qualify riders automatically for an LT Pro Number. 2025 and 2026 results both count for 2027.

Life Time has denoted seven races as LT Pro Qualifiers, where a top result can earn you an LT Pro Number. The key word here is can, because you need to finish top-three and within 10% of the winner’s time.

Cutoff times for both LT Pro and LT Pro Qualifiers can be found here .

Racers can also earn an LT Pro number through these alternate pathways, though these will be reviewed by a committee and are not automatic. The committee is made up of Life Time race and series staff.

There are 19 non-Life Time events that offer racers a chance to qualify for an LT Pro Number.

In addition to qualifying with finish time, or a combination of overall position and finish time, racers who win their age group overall in a Life Time qualifying race can also apply for an LT Pro Number. Racers with an LT Pro number are not required to race pro and can opt to race age group instead.

You can read more about qualification and apply here . Applying is free and racers are allowed to reapply with every qualifying result they earn. Qualification is good for that calendar year, after which racers will need to either reapply or qualify automatically for 2028 based on 2027 results. You will hear back from the committee within a week.

French para-cyclist Thomas Peyroton-Dartet has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for EPO at September’s world championships in Huntsville, Alabama, the International Testing Agency announced Thursday.

Peyroton-Dartet — a C3 category athlete — is provisionally suspended while the case proceeds. No final sanction has been announced.

The finding came from a sample collected September 5 during the UCI Para-cycling Road World Championships. The ITA, which runs the UCI’s independent anti-doping program , is handling the case .

Just two days later, he won gold in the C3 road race ahead of a pair of chasing Spanish riders.

Peyroton-Dartet, 41, also won gold in the C3 time trial and silver in the C1-3 road race in the Paris 2024 Olympic Games.

EPO needs little introduction for cycling fans.

It stimulates red blood cell production, increasing the oxygen available to working muscles and boosting endurance. This is not the first time that EPO has been detected in para-cycling.

Poland’s Marcin Polak received a four-year ban in 2022 after three samples collected in 2021 tested positive. His results during the affected period were wiped out.

Factor Bikes is heading back to the men’s WorldTour, and Bahrain Victorious is changing bikes again.

The team confirmed a new partnership beginning in 2027, bringing Factor back to cycling’s top men’s division after a season away following its split with Israel-Premier Tech at the end of 2025 .

Factor secures a place in the WorldTour and a guaranteed spot in the Tour de France .

“Personally, I find it fitting that Factor was born in the UK, and next year, in our 10th anniversary year, Factor will be back at the highest level of racing in the UK at the Tour de France,” said Factor founder Rob Gitelis.

Friday’s announcement did not specify details, but the deal means Factor’s aero-focused Ostro VAM and lightweight O2 VAM climbing bike will be back in the men’s WorldTour.

The company will supply Bahrain across the grand tours and classics with its full fleet of bikes.

For Bahrain, the deal means another equipment switch as its relationship with Bianchi ends and will mark its third bike supplier in as many years.

Factor’s one-year absence from the men’s WorldTour didn’t mean it disappeared from the peloton. Like most top brands, Factor’s DNA is spread across the pack.

The brand supplied Women’s WorldTour team Human Powered Health in 2026, and backed Modern Adventure Pro Cycling , the men’s ProTeam founded by George Hincapie. The brand will be co-sponsor for the team’s second season .

The Bahrain deal — which neither the team or Factor shared publicly how long it will last — brings the company back into the full men’s WorldTour calendar, with all the exposure, demands, pressure, and equipment scrutiny that comes with it.

“At Factor, we have always believed that racing at the pinnacle of the sport is fundamental to who we are. It’s where our ideas are challenged, where our engineering is tested, and where we continue to push ourselves forward,” Gitelis said. “We see this partnership as much more than supplying bikes to a professional team. It’s an opportunity to work together, to innovate, and to compete against the very best. We are incredibly excited about what we can achieve together from 2027.”

Factor previously supplied Israel-Premier Tech from 2020 through 2025, putting its bikes under riders like Chris Froome and Michael Woods. That relationship ended amid the controversy surrounding the team’s Israeli identity, that came to a head in the Vuelta a España as protesters disrupted the race.

Factor first entered the men’s WorldTour with AG2R La Mondiale in 2016, when Romain Bardet rode its bikes onto the Tour podium.

For Bahrain’s riders and mechanics, the agreement means getting used to yet another fleet of bikes. Bahrain raced Bianchi only one season after switching over from Merida in 2026.

Top riders like Matej Mohorič and Lenny Martinez will soon have the bikes.

The announcement did not specify which Factor models the team will race, or detail the wider component package.

Bahrain managing director Milan Eržen said the agreement means more direct input from riders and performance staff in the development process.

“We have found a fantastic partner in Factor, a brand that shares our performance ethos and our ambition to be the best,” Eržen said. “Factor is continuously innovating on the bike, with a huge focus on performance, which will enable our riders to have one of the best setups in the peloton.”

Work is already underway behind the scenes, with the team’s first pre-season training camps set for November and December.

I travel with a bike more than most people, and it terrifies me every single time. After having a Look 795 Blade RS arrive broken in a Scicon AeroComfort case, I went down a deep rabbit hole—talking to the TSA and picking apart the fine print of airline contracts of carriage. Since then, I’ve learned even more by talking to the people who actually design bike luggage. Despite still being absolutely terrified of landing with a broken bike, I’ve learned a lot of info that rarely gets talked about. Here’s what I know about flying with a bike right now.

When you check baggage on a flight, you are agreeing to a contract of carriage. You might occasionally have to explicitly sign a waiver, but typically, you’ll hear nothing about it. You’ve still agreed to it, and if something happens to your bike, you are bound by those terms.

This contract outlines the liability an airline accepts when taking your property. Look carefully, because some airlines exclude bike liability completely, while others cap it at a specific amount that likely won’t cover a replacement frame. That cap drops even lower on international flights. The contract will also dictate what type of case is considered acceptable, and most airlines specify a hard case.

On top of airline rules, the TSA will almost always open your bag because it’s too large to be scanned. When I spoke to Sean Harbaugh, a supervisory TSA officer with 20 years of experience, he told me their biggest request is that cyclists stop packing extra gear and clothing into the case alongside the bike.

Add all of this up, and the reality is far less black and white than the airlines want you to believe—a gray area I’ll explain in a moment. But first, if your bike gets damaged, expect a huge fight to get a payout, and it will likely be less than you need. Regardless of the amount though, if you want any chance of succeeding, you must check your bike at the airport before you leave. You cannot make a claim once you walk out those doors. Open the case, check carefully for damage, and start the claim immediately if you find a problem. During that process, explicitly request that the security video of the TSA checking your bike be preserved. The inspection is always on video, but that footage will be overwritten unless you demand they pull it.

This is pretty obvious, and it’s what everyone thinks is the issue. Baggage handlers generally do not care about your bike. Sometimes they are outright hostile with it, but typically, they just don’t care. The bag will almost always get flipped on its side, and it will sometimes get slammed on the ground, a luggage cart, or a belt. Make sure whatever case you use will protect your bike from this treatment.

If your bars come off and you can fold them down, things are pretty easy. Even a cardboard box will typically work, although my favorite option for this scenario is the Topeak PakGo X. The real challenge comes when you are dealing with a modern bike and can’t take your bars off.

If that’s what you are up against, look for something that keeps your case from being crushed from the sides. The Orucase Sentinel is an incredible option that uses a rather genius internal aluminum roll cage. It protects the controls by running a rigid expansion bar through the drops that secures into place inside the case. I have a friend who actually uses the Scicon that broke my bike, but he uses PVC pipes to create an anti-crush system very similar to what Orucase is doing. Of course, a more traditional hard case will win out if you are only looking at what it takes to protect your bike from the baggage handlers.

After I had my bike broken, I swore I’d never fly with another soft case. Then I started using the Orucase Sentinel and had a conversation with the founder of Orucase, Isaac Howe. I’ve talked to him for years about the theory of bike cases, but recently we talked about what actually constitutes a “hard case.”

In talking to him, I realized I’d made a mistake in blindly believing the airlines. It seems like what the contract of carriage means is that you need a giant plastic or aluminum vault like a Shokbox or a Bike Box Alan. The reality is that no one has ever litigated it. If you have a soft outer material that covers a rigid internal structure, you can argue that it is still a hard case. Should someone go to court with that line of reasoning, they might well win. No one will actually go to court, though, so my advice is to think carefully about what you say if you ever make a claim. Your case could well qualify as a hard case, so don’t make the mistake of calling it a soft case.

The reason all of this matters is that you aren’t just protecting your bike from baggage handlers. If you were, a traditional hard case would be the undisputed answer. Instead, Howe told me that one of the hardest things to design for is the TSA. You meticulously pack your bike, everything is safe inside a hard outer shell, and then a TSA agent opens it and doesn’t bother putting it back together correctly. You might end up with a broken bike even though the case was strong enough to withstand anything a baggage handler could throw at it.

For my most recent trip, I ended up choosing the Post Carry Co. Loomer for this exact reason. It helped that Factor CEO Calvin Chan told me he carries the Factor ONE Bugatti edition bikes all over the world in that case, but it was also just the way it works. It’s essentially a hard case, but its simple closure system and the ease of seeing the bike made me think the TSA might be less apt to mess it up.…

When it comes to going fast on a bike, aerodynamics is the modern answer. Weight matters, but we’ve long since established that aero wins out. So just go buy a new aero bike and a set of deep wheels… oh wait, that costs a fortune, plus you might actually prefer the snappy feel of a lightweight climbing bike anyway.

There’s another option though. The reality is that an aero helmet can save as much drag as those 50mm wheels you’ve been dreaming about, and it might even save more watts than a dedicated aero frame. That level of free speed is exactly why I’m paying attention to this deal on the Lazer Vento KinetiCore; pro-level aero helmets rarely see deep discounts, making a 35% price drop well worth a look.

Lazer built the Vento KinetiCore to be fast, and it seems the brand succeeded. If you look at independent aero testing, the Vento sits right in the same tier as the MET Manta and the Kask Utopia Y, while not being far off the Sweet Protection Tucker. Aero numbers are finicky, though. You also have to live with a helmet, and the things that really set the Vento KinetiCore apart are the quality-of-life details.

Instead of adding a separate plastic slip-plane liner inside the helmet for rotational impact protection, Lazer molded its “KinetiCore” crumple zones directly into the EPS foam. Removing that internal liner leaves huge, unobstructed Venturi channels for airflow, making it breathe exceptionally well for an aero helmet.

Lazer also uses a unique “ScrollSys” treadmill-like belt on the back of the helmet instead of a traditional dial fit system. It sits flat, which makes it comfortable against the back of your head and very ponytail-friendly.

Headlights for road riding need to do different things for different people. For some, it’s just about the bare minimum: something for cars to see and to illuminate the road so drivers can spot upcoming potholes. For others, it is a key tool in their stable: big lights that power early or late rides that salvage exercise in the hectic pace of a busy life.

For most of my life, I have been the former. My headlights have been just enough to be seen in the dawn and dusk. As I have gotten older, however, that has changed. Lights have become more important as my time to ride has shifted to the early morning hours that are the bread and butter of Phoenix, Arizona, riding.

Lights are now essential kit that I have to think about differently. It is technology I need more from.

Exposure Lights has built a brand upon that attitude. The small UK-based shop has grown to prominence with lights that match reliable performance, long battery life, and sleek aesthetics.

Nowhere has this been more obvious than with the brand’s new Strada 13 RS light. As I have ventured deeper into the night as the seasons have changed, the Strada has been a fantastic companion in getting much more out of night riding.

Despite a size that is typically reserved for off-road-focused lights, the Strada 13 is a purpose-built tool for road riding. Chief among those features is the lights’ auto-dimming AKTiv technology.

AKTiv is automatically configured on the Strada 13 and is set to dim its beam when it senses an oncoming car. The AKTiv technology has been a fixture on previous models, but the new Strada has two sensors that allow for increased precision. On rides, this makes for rapid adjustments that keep my hands on the bars and the driver from being blasted by a few hundred lumens of light.

Speaking of lumens, while it might seem that the bigger light is there for more lumens, that isn’t exactly the case. Exposure does pack more lumens in smaller packages, like the Diablo off-road light. The size of the light is more for the battery life and the added road-based functionality.

That battery has been a huge plus in my riding. While I haven’t yet ridden through the night with it yet—which would certainly be possible for the Strada 13 on one charge—the longevity of the battery has been a huge benefit.

Compared to smaller lights, I have been thrilled by the combination of a powerful beam and the set-it-and-forget-it battery life. Through a full week of riding, with more than a few hours before dark, the light can stay on with no issues.

To put it plainly, 217g is a lot of weight for a light. Part of me loves a small, easy-to-add headlight for road riding. The Exposure’s Sirius 11 road light is a mere 90g, and it can still kick up to 1,300 lumens. Yet, it doesn’t have the same adjustability, beam range, and most significantly, battery life.

Previously, if I had the choice of a light the size of the Sirius and the Strada for the fast group ride, I would have picked the Sirius every time. Now, the choice is not so clear-cut, although if I were measuring my night riding time in minutes and not hours, I would still perhaps pick the Sirius for its weight and sleek size.

The other real wonky aspect of the light is the single-button interface. It takes a bit of trial and error to figure out how the sequencing of button presses yields the desired results. Even so, I find that I don’t always get the light to do what I want straightaway. There is a way to bring some of the light controls and displays to any head unit to make that functionality simpler. But, straight out of the box, it is less than intuitive.

The Strada is perhaps most useful as a piece of kit that is low maintenance, easy to use, and easy to swap between bikes if you have multiple mounts.

The light has two attachments, one for a 31.9-diameter round bar and the other for an action mount that can be attached to an integrated computer mount, and both are stripped down but sturdy. Both mounts put the light further forward, away from the bike to provide a better position to illuminate the periphery of the road. That said, with the added weight, be sure to check the weight tolerances of the mounts before using the light since it could push the weight limit in some cases.

All of my riding with the light thus far has been with the action mount attached to the bar mount for the Trek Domane I have been testing with. It has been incredibly easy to use, easy to set up, and the big light almost disappears underneath the computer mount and bar. Out of sight, out of mind rings very true for a big headlight.

Lastly, with a USB-C cable port, the light is always easy to find a charger for. It can also be easily flipped and used to top up other electronics in a pinch. While the battery might last a while, charging it takes much less time. With the optimal cable, the Strada will fully charge in two hours.

The Exposure Strada 13 RS is for two types of riders: those who ride at night multiple times a week, and those who will measure their time riding in the dark in hours rather than minutes. If you fit those categories, this is one of the best tech adds you can make to boost the quality of your rides. It is good enough to be that transformative.

I never set out to sing the praises of 160mm cranks. Having already made the transition from 170mm to 165mm cranks several years ago, I felt like I had reached the promised land of power and performance. There was nothing more to gain. Plus, as a 5-foot-6 cyclist, how much shorter could I reasonably go? Apparently another 5 millimeters.

A lot of times innovations from the pro peloton don’t always make sense for us mere mortals. This one, however, is an exception. Shortening your crank length is a pro move that’s worth paying attention to, because the benefits aren’t just theoretical; they’re practical for riders of all levels.

To get into the details I met with Cesar Correa, founder of San Francisco’s Cassette Fit Studio who has been fitting bikes since 2013, to see why more riders should start to think small. Correa has been recommending shorter cranks for years.

“Crank-wise, I do think it’s very important to go shorter,” he told me. When I rolled into his studio on a Canyon Endurace with its stock 160mm cranks, his reaction was considerably more enthusiastic than mine had been. “When you brought in that bike and we saw that it came with 160s, it was like, that’s amazing,” he says.

Shorter cranks mean shorter virtual circles that your foot is tracing with each pedal rotation. Since your knee doesn’t rise as high at the top of each stroke, you can compensate for this positioning change by bumping up your saddle height.

As a general rule, when you shorten your cranks you raise your saddle height roughly the difference. So if you’re dropping down 5mm from 170mm to 165mm, you would bump up your saddle by 5mm. Give or take.

“That’s the easy way to do it,” says Correa. “But it could add up to about anywhere from eight, sometimes even 10mm different.” Correa says the final adjustment depends on the rider, their biomechanics, and can involve moving the saddle both up and back.

And there’s another catch. “When you move to shorter cranks, you raise the saddle, then some people tend to just drop the handlebars lower, but that means your hips are still going to close,” Correa told me. “So you’re not actually doing anything different.”

So simply going shorter doesn’t give you permission to slam your stem. “You can achieve a bit more drop with the shorter cranks, but it’s not as aggressive as people think.” It’s about creating more room between your knee and torso, which can give you more freedom to find an aerodynamic position without closing your hips back up.

A lower knee raise creates a more open hip angle. But what does that actually mean? The best analogy is a squat at the gym. A closed hip angle is the equivalent of doing a partial squat, which really burns out your smaller hip flexor muscles and doesn’t allow you to produce a lot of power.

Whereas a more open hip angle is akin to doing a full squat—it produces more power and recruits more muscles. From Correa’s perspective, the important part is simply giving your hip and knee more room to move. “When you go shorter in cranks, especially if you have knee issues, your knees are not going to have to bend as much,” he says. “They’re a lot freer.” And it’s something he can actually see during a fit. “Your foot gets through the stroke a lot better with shorter cranks,” Correa says. That extra room can also help the knee track more naturally through the pedal stroke rather than forcing your body to compensate for a position it doesn’t particularly like. For me it just felt more relaxed. Like sitting in a really comfy chair. The body just fell into place and the legs were able to turn over almost effortlessly. I could maintain a high cadence, turning over the pedals without much effort, and ticking up the hills like it was no big deal.

To be clear, shorter cranks don’t magically give you more watts. But the shorter arms change your riding position, and that’s where the magic happens. It all comes down to which muscles you can recruit. And on shorter cranks, you can tap into some big ones.

When you pedal through the power phase of your stroke, between 12 o’clock and 5 o’clock, you can engage your quads more and shift that load into a more efficient power transfer. The short cranks and more open hip angle allow this to happen. Now you’re shifting the load towards your quads, engaging bigger muscles that are more resilient and ideal for endurance efforts. It’s more efficient, more sustainable, and allows you to feel comfortable for longer. I immediately felt this on climbs, like I magically had another gear. I could feel more engagement from my quads, not just my glutes. It’s a little bit of an odd sensation at first, but you quickly get used to it and before long, you’re spinning easier doing some of your most efficient climbing ever.

A 160mm circle versus a 175mm circle is a significant difference, and that means the rotations your foot will make are directly translated. You’ve instantly reduced the arc in which your foot travels across each revolution. It’s a tighter circle which means you can spin faster.

For me, that’s exactly what I noticed on the 160s. Climbing felt easier. My pedal stroke felt quicker, and holding a higher cadence felt more natural than my 165s. And there are other benefits too.

Office workers of the world listen up, this one is for you. “If you’re someone who sits at a desk all day, you’re gonna have the tightest hips in the world,” Correa says. “So shorter cranks will help with that.” Reducing that demand on your hip flexors could also help limit some of the stress that builds up over a long ride. Then there are the knees.

For Correa, watching what happens to the knee at the very top of every pedal stroke is key. “If you can not bend the knee at the top of the stroke as much, that will help, because it’s always that top of the stroke where that bend will cause a lot of issues.”…

Today, Zwift is launching Zwift Plus. This new premium tier pushes the monthly cost to $29.99, with a discounted yearly option at $299.99. In exchange for the upcharge, you unlock two core upgrades: real-world video routes and adaptive coaching.

Zwift considers this a massive milestone, which is why I recently went to Moab to celebrate the video-based routes ahead of launch. The concept was to ride the route indoors, then ride it outdoors to see how perfectly they matched. Unfortunately, we caught the tail end of a Pacific hurricane, so I only got to drive the route and ride it inside. Still, the big reveal ended up feeling almost anti-climactic—but in the best way possible.

The inside perfectly matches the real world, but you still get all the Zwift details you are used to. Zwift lays the graphics seamlessly into high-resolution and high frame rate footage. I rode the Tron bike in Arches National Park, and while it sadly doesn’t glow on the road, the wheels sit perfectly on the video road and the speed adjusts as you ride without ever breaking the illusion. It’s underwhelming, but only because it’s really good and feels like a natural extension of what Zwift already does. If you’ve used Rouvy, which Zwift now owns, this is better.

Personally, though, I don’t find the video-based routes all that much of a draw. They provide more variety, and that’s great, but Zwift already adds routes all the time and anyone who’s used Zwift knows the team is great at recreating real-life locations. What this launch is really all about is coaching, and that’s where the real magic is.

Part of why the team at Zwift considered this launch such a high-stakes proposition is that it’s a price increase, and that always comes with baggage. You could even consider the addition of the video routes to the Zwift Plus plan as a sort of tiered pricing structure where, all of a sudden, you have to pay for more routes. That’s not really true, but I can understand the hesitation.

I think part of why I don’t see that as an issue is because I don’t find the video routes to be the major news here. They are additional content, and as someone who will likely chew through every single additional badge Zwift offers this winter, that’s nice, but also not a big deal. Instead, I see this as a pretty clear value proposition of $10 a month for structured training.

With that in mind, my favorite thing about Zwift Plus is that I see it as a product that is going to consolidate the structured training market. I believe this will be a big hit to TrainerRoad, and I think that for many people, Zwift Plus will represent a net decrease in monthly subscriptions.

The reasons for this are pretty simple: structured training has to be good enough, and it has to create an environment where the user actually follows the plan. Before this launch, Zwift was mostly failing at both of those requirements.

Zwift already had training plans; they just weren’t engaging, they weren’t reactive, and they were widely considered to be not that great. With Zwift Plus, the first correction was the quality of the plans, and to address that, Zwift brought on Ryan Cooper.

If you aren’t familiar with the name, Ryan Cooper is the founder of Best Bike Split and the former Chief Scientist at TrainingPeaks. To understand why his involvement is so important, you have to look at what Best Bike Split actually does. It is a predictive physics engine that takes a rider’s specific power profile, weight, and aerodynamics, layers it over the exact elevation of a race course, and calculates exactly how many watts that rider should push on every single segment to finish as fast as possible without blowing up.

That is the level of data-driven modeling he brings to Zwift, and it is exactly why the brand is very careful to call this new coaching system “machine learning” rather than “AI.” Right now, AI is a marketing buzzword. When most people hear it, they picture a chatbot scraping the internet and hallucinating a generic training plan based on a text prompt.

Machine learning is different. It relies on math and datasets. In this case, Cooper’s algorithms were trained on the anonymized power and heart rate data of millions of Zwift riders, combined with peer-reviewed sports science. The system isn’t guessing or estimating based on what it read online. It uses actual machine learning to recognize patterns in your specific history, power data, and daily fatigue, and then mathematically calculates exactly what you need to do today to actually get faster.

This means Zwift has now solved the quality problem that TrainerRoad has so far always held as an advantage. But the raw quality of workouts is actually somewhat secondary in real life. You need not only quality workouts, but you need workouts that people will complete, and this is where Zwift has something no one else does.

Zwift controls everything about where you ride your bike, and that means the Zwift Plus workout plan has options. Once you set up your plan, the system will recommend an ever-changing variety in terms of how you complete a workout. My favorite example was actually the first day of the 12-week plan I started, when I was scheduled for a route rather than a set of intervals.…

The grands départs of the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France are being slated as the most expensive bike races ever held.

British journalist Jeremy Whittle reported last week that the UK government will invest a total of £65m GBP (~$85m USD) into hosting the grands départs of next year’s Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes .

Spanning six days of racing across Scotland, Wales, and England, each stage will cost a staggering equivalent of £11m (~$15m).

And that’s not the only wild expense associated with the Tour’s British start.

The opening ceremony and team presentation of the men’s race will be fully ticketed, with the most premium seats being sold for £99 a pop. That’s just north of $130 for the privilege of seeing Tadej Pogačar and his comrades doing some bemused waving on a big stage.

For race organizer ASO, an overseas start is a lucrative money spinner. It charges host nations millions of Euros for the honor. In return, hosts can use the Tour de France as a promotional platform and legacy investment.

However, next year’s grands départs – the men’s 28th overseas jaunt and the women’s third – will be extraordinary business.

Whittle reported eye-watering expenses associated with the privilege of being the first nation to host a partnered men’s and women’s event.

Running out of Edinburgh on July 2 for the men’s race and from Leeds on July 30 for the Femmes, Whittle called the six stages of the $85m USD carnival “the most expensive bike races ever held.”

For context, the 2014 UK grand départ reportedly cost the British government £29.4m.

While it’s comparing apples to oranges, the full cost of the 11-day multi-format Glasgow “super worlds” in 2023 nudged toward £63m.

But how can a few hundred kilometers of the Tour de France be so costly?

The hosting fees paid over to the race organizer are huge, and they’re only the start.

ASO is thought to have charged around €10m euros (~£8m or $11m) for the rights to host recent grands départ s in Florence (2024) and Barcelona (2026). The hosting charges for 2027 are unknown.

After that, costs associated with staging the biggest bike races in the world include security, road resurfacing, preparing local infrastructure, and supporting all the random side-events that pop up when the Tour comes to town.

The UK Government has projected economic benefits of more than £150m from the combined 2027 men’s and women’s race.

One particular side-event of the 2027 Tour de France has garnered particular interest – and stirred significant controversy – in recent weeks.

The opening ceremony and team presentation of the men’s Tour on Wednesday 30 June will be fully ticketed, and admission ain’t cheap.

Tickets for the event on the esplanade outside Edinburgh Castle span from £27 ($36) for “bring the binoculars” seats high in the stands to £99 ($130) for primo spots.

Pogačar and the peloton will trundle on and off the stage as part of a mash-up ceremony that includes a show by The Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo. The traditional Scottish event is a bagpipes ‘n’ kilts show including music, dance, and rock concert lighting.

Details of the Tour de France Femmes opening ceremony have not yet been confirmed.

It’s rare, but not unprecedented, for Tour de France team presentations to be ticketed.

However, the past three, held in suitably spectacular settings in Barcelona, Lille, and Florence, were all free to attend.

News that next year’s team presentation will be ticketed has, of course, stirred debate.

The Tour de France does sell itself on being “the biggest free sporting event in the world,” after all.

When Whittle enquired about the charges as part of his Substack report, a representative argued for the event’s extraordinary nature.

“This isn’t a standard team presentation,” a Grand Départ GB told Whittle. “By partnering with The Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, we’re creating a one-off event that fans won’t have seen before at a grand départ, and ticketing reflects that.

“As with any team presentation, the riders will take a route through the city before arriving at Edinburgh Castle, in this case from Holyrood Palace via the Royal Mile to the castle, which will be completely unticketed,” they added.

The representative also reminded Whittle every kilometer of all three stages of the men’s grand départ will be open access.

“The race itself stays free,” they said. “Spectators will have free access to more than 900km of roadside across both grands départs, and we expect people to come out in their millions to cheer on the world’s best male and female riders.”

If the ticket fees aren’t steep enough to put you off the prospect of some traditional Scottish dance and some bemused pro cyclists, tickets go on general sale here on October 30.

Modern Adventure Pro Cycling is sizing up for 2027 after its breakout debut season.

Last week, George Hincapie’s budding team revealed a flood of new signings that will expand its debut roster of 21 riders to 24 for its sophomore year.

WorldTour veteran Jonas Rutsch, former U.S. national U23 champion Owen Cole, and reigning Australian champion Patrick Eddy all join the team for 2027.

Meanwhile, the exit door has been kept shut. As of late October, no riders have confirmed they will leave the new American team.

Multiple U.S. national champion Quinn Simmons had been repeatedly linked to Hincapie’s ambitious young project. However, the rumor mill has slowed in recent weeks. The 25-year-old’s long-term deal with Lidl-Trek makes any gamble with Modern Adventure seem highly unlikely.

Simmons or not, the arrival of three new riders in 2027 – a 16 percent expansion in the roster – signals clear intent.

In its rookie 2026 season, the team won five times, raced across continents, and saw a marquee invite to Paris-Roubaix.

In 2027, with added financial heft from new co-title sponsor Factor Bikes, Hincapie wants more from a team he hopes to take toward the Tour de France.

“I wanna look back in five, six years from now and go, ‘this is where we started,’” Hincapie told Velo earlier this season. “From basically ‘Bad News Bears’ to building to be one of the best teams in the world.”

Rutsch and Eddy are the household international names of Modern Adventure’s three new signings.

Rutsch spent seven years in the WorldTour and has twice hit the top-11 at Paris-Roubaix.

Eddy rebounded from losing a spot in the WorldTour by outfoxing two Jayco-AlUla riders at Aussie nationals and dominating the Conti circuit with Team Brennan.

Modern Adventure’s biggest hopes might lie with Cole, however.

The 22-year-old Californian won the U23 U.S. road race aged 19, and this year finished top-six in both the national U23 road race and time trial.

Cole spent a year in the UAE Emirates-XRG devo system in 2024 before he reinforced his status as one of USA’s brightest talents in his two years with Team Winston Salem-Flow.

“We’re excited to welcome Owen to the team. He’s a talented young rider with a bright future, and we’re excited to help him develop,” Hincapie said.

“Supporting young, talented American riders is important to us and part of our mission, and we look forward to helping Owen reach the highest level of the sport.”

Cole is the 13th American rider on Modern Adventure’s 24-rider squad for 2027, maintaining its stated mission of having at least a 50 percent American roster.

Who is the best rider in pro cycling? The Velo d’Or prize tries to answer that.

The road season is over, but there’s still some prizes to dole out with cycling’s most prestigious and sometimes controversial awards.

L’Équipe revealed the nominees Thursday, with the winners set to collect their trophies November 28 at the Fairmont Monte Carlo in Monaco in a posh, Oscar night-style party.

Some of these are no-brainers. Demi Vollering will be the overwhelming favorite after winning a second yellow jersey and her first rainbow title.

Tadej Pogačar could match Alberto Contador as the all-time winner of four times. He’ll face off against the likes of world champion Brandon McNulty, French phenom Paul Seixas, and Vuelta winner Enric Mas.

There’s more hardware up for grabs this year, too. Four new awards will honor the best male and female sprinters and rookies, with fans deciding the rookie winners.

Created by Vélo Magazine in 1992, the Vélo d’Or – the “golden bike” in French — is cycling’s answer to soccer’s Ballon d’Or.

Winners are chosen by an international panel of cycling journalists based on wins, star power, versatility, and panache . (Full disclosure: I’m on that jury. And whittling down the winners can be harder than you’d think.)

But will Pogačar’s injury-shortened season undercut his chances of winning? Let’s dive in.

This one should be a sure bet. Vollering dominated every race she started, and won her second yellow jersey and her first world title.

Lorena Wiebes could pick up some votes for her dominance in the sprints, but she’ll be a lock for that new award. Spain’s Paula Blasi — who recently penned a blockbuster deal with Movistar — could be an outsider.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney — winner on Mont Ventoux — and Marlen Reusser are other contenders, but this one’s all but certain for DemVol .

A stand-alone women’s category was created in 2022, and Vollering could become the first repeat winner.

The big name missing? Defending winner Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, although she’s still in the running for the French women’s award.

Even with crashing out of the Vuelta a España and missing the worlds, Pogačar will probably win again, but his stiffest competition could come from within his UAE Emirates-XRG team bus.

Isaac del Toro and newly crowned world champion McNulty — the only American nominated — join him on the shortlist, giving UAE three of the 10 spots.

How to measure up Pogačar’s season? King Pog absolutely dominated the 2026 season, and only a superb Wout van Aert could deny him Paris-Roubaix. A crash doesn’t diminish his fantastic season, but his absence did open the doors for many on this list.

Mas brings a Vuelta title, while Seixas gets a seat alongside some of the biggest names of the past decade. Remco Evenepoel was unstoppable against the clock, McNulty won America’s first rainbow since the 1990s, and Van Aert could be an emotional favorite.

The classics awards give the one-day specialists their own moment on the stage, although there’s plenty of crossover with the main event.

This sometimes can get sloppy. With today’s top riders so versatile, it’s hard to pigeon-hole a rider like Pogačar into one category.

A few years ago, fans were outraged when Mathieu van der Poel was named best classics rider and Pogačar won the overall prize. Can that happen again this year?

All five men’s finalists also made the overall shortlist. On the women’s side, Lotte Kopecky and Puck Pieterse are hoping to win based on what they delivered on a single afternoon.

Women : Franziska Koch, Lotte Kopecky, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, Puck Pieterse and Demi Vollering.

Men : Remco Evenepoel, Tadej Pogačar, Paul Seixas, Wout van Aert and Mathieu van der Poel.

The fast finishers finally see their own trophies this year. About time, some might say.

The new awards give sprinting its due, especially with sprinters increasingly seeing fewer opportunities to shine as grand tours have become more challenging over the past two decades (though the men’s 2027 Tour de France sees a revival of sorts).

Wiebes is the only rider on both the women’s sprint and overall shortlists. Matthew Brennan has two chances here, with nominations for sprinting and the rookie prize.

Women : Elisa Balsamo, Lara Gillespie, Charlotte Kool, Nienke Veenhoven and Lorena Wiebes.

Men : Matthew Brennan, Paul Magnier, Tim Merlier, Jonathan Milan and Jasper Philipsen.

Want an actual vote? The new rookie awards are where fans get their say .

And “rookie” comes with some fine print. Riders qualify through standout performances on their first appearance at a grand tour, monument, or world championships, so they don’t necessarily have to be first-year pros.

Paula Blasi and Seixas are also nominated for the main awards.

Women : Paula Blasi, Célia Gery and Isabella Holmgren.

Men : Matthew Brennan, Jakob Omrzel and Paul Seixas.

The French rider awards means the hometown stars won’t leave empty-handed, with Seixas appearing on his fourth shortlist of the evening.

Women : Juliette Berthet, Marion Bunel, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, Célia Gery and Cédrine Kerbaol.

Men : Dorian Godon, Romain Grégoire, Paul Magnier, Lenny Martinez and Paul Seixas.

For the main Vélo d’Or awards, each journalist ranks five riders from the respective 10-person lists. First gets five points, second gets four, and so on down to one point for fifth.

Sounds straightforward until you’re staring at the ballot and trying to decide who gets left off.

The ceremony will hand out 12 awards, including para-cycling honors, and will air live on L’Équipe ’s free-to-air French television channel.

I’ve got some decisions to make. Who’s in your top five?
