Tadej Pogačar heard the Tour de France director questioning his appetite for risk after his brutal crash at the Vuelta a España and said, “Hold my beer.”

Fan footage shot last week showing the 28-year-old slalom through traffic in busy Monaco suggests Pogi has bounced back confident as ever.

The videos, filmed Thursday and shared on Instagram by French amateur Noah Alfrink, are a white-knuckle watch.

The grabs show Pogačar resplendent in his UAE Emirates-XRG jersey cutting lanes, squeezing alongside buses, and flirting with the bumpers of moving cars in the hectic roads of his adopted home.

The videos went viral this weekend and have drawn a very mixed response.

Not even the GOATed fan favorite is spared from criticism of “reckless riding,” a “lack of respect for safety,” and a whole lot more. The 19-year-old Alfrink isn’t shown mercy either, as commentators hit out at the latest example of fans “ cyclo-stalking ” superstar riders.

“I don’t know which is dumber, Pogačar, or the one following him,” reads one comment.

Imágenes de un aficionado siguiendo a Tadej Pogačar durante su entrenamiento de ayer por Mónaco ➡️ El esloveno iba vestido con el maillot del UAE 📹 @noah_alfr pic.twitter.com/fs0nr6sbxI

Only one day earlier, Tour de France director Christian Prudhomme pondered whether Pogačar would be the same after his brutal crash at the Vuelta a España.

The 28-year-old broke his collarbone, a vertebra, and suffered a concussion when he hit the tarmac hard in late August.

It cost the Tour de France dominator the chance to win the Vuelta’s red jersey, defend his titles at the world and European championships, and win a sixth Il Lombardia.

Speaking to L’Equipe on Thursday, Prudhomme questioned whether the crash pierced Pogačar’s sense of invincibility, too.

“The real question for me – and I obviously wish him well – is how well he’ll have recovered from his very, very, very serious crash in the Vuelta a España,” Prudhomme said. “His talent lies not only in his physical superiority, but also in his riding skills.

“His descent of the Tourmalet last summer was mind-blowing and jaw-dropping,” Prudhomme told L’Equipe . “As you get older, after such a massive crash, are you still the same person? Do you take as many risks?”

Prudhomme spoke the day he and ASO unleashed a route for the 2027 Tour de France that’s been labeled “anti-Pogačar.”

The race director suggested 71km of time trialing might not be Pogačar’s only problem when he defends his yellow jersey next July.

“There are certainly questions lingering after his crash,” Prudhomme said. “Whether it has left its mark on him and what the consequences will be.

Pogačar seems to have brushed off any mental hangover of his 60kph crash just fine.

Some may say his comfort on the bike might be a little too good.

Pogačar, his teammates, and the staff at UAE Emirates-XRG meet next for a 2027 planning and admin camp. It doesn’t look like Pogačar will be nervous in the wheels of any group rides.

Remco Evenepoel has had a interesting off season, visiting the US and also attending the Serie A match between Como 1907 and AS Roma in October 11, 2026. (Photo: Mairo Cinquetti/NurPhoto via Getty Images) (Photo: NurPhoto)

It’s the off season, a time to recharge, but that hasn’t stopped Olympic and world TT champion Remco Evenepoel from logging more training kilometers and scoping out the route of a major objective.

The Belgian is currently in California visiting the headquarters of bike sponsor Specialized and has used that time to build relationships and to work on some things which could pay off well in 2027 and beyond.

On Sunday he put in a 65.34km ride, starting near Griffith Park and the LA Zoo, and taking in parts of the TT course for the 2028 LA Olympic Games.

The full route has not yet been released but he still used the time to familiarize himself with the area and with whatever course details he has been able to ascertain.

The ride then concluded close to the beach at Santa Monica.

Evenepoel has been busy since arriving in LA, doing what he described as a LA Jetlag and Sunrise Run on Saturday and then taking in a 48.08km social ride with Specialized.

Photos from the latter were posted by @Shreddypendergrass, and showed Evenepoel doing a group ride in his European road champion’s jersey.

Also present were FDJ Suez riders Demi Vollering and Kate Courtney . The world champ and US national champion are also Specialized-sponsored athletes.

According to Sporza, the trip will see Evenepoel—and presumably the other pros—do additional wind tunnel testing at the Specialized HQ in Morgan Hill.

The Belgian recently spent some days at a Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe training camp, working on plans for next season.

He had his best season to date in 2026, notching up 15 victories including the worlds TT and European championships road race, and taking the runner-up slot in the Tour de France.

Vollering had an even more impressive year, taking 16 wins in 33 days of competition. Her triumphs included the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, the Giro d’Italia Women, the world road championships, Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the Tour of Flanders and more.

Both are highly ambitious and, like Courtney, are using this time to work towards even bigger results next year.

Tadej Pogačar appeared on course to win the Vuelta a España until his stage 8 crash (Photo: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty Images) (Photo: Alexander Hassenstein)

Tadej Pogačar has revealed he was more seriously injured than first thought following his crash in the Vuelta a España , with not one but three spinal fractures caused by his fall on stage 8.

The five-time Tour de France winner said the extent of his injuries only became clear in mid-October, bringing home the risks he faced of death or paralysis.

“Two weeks ago, I was in Slovenia and I went to do another CT scan. I knew I had a C7 fracture, but then we saw I had two more broken vertebrae, the T1 and T2,” he told The Athletic , part of the New York Times.

“At that moment, I was happy I didn’t do the European Championships, which had been my initial goal.

“When I saw I had three broken vertebrae? I’m just happy to be alive, actually, or just to be standing.”

The C7, T1 and T2 vertebrae are located in the lower neck and upper back.

Pogačar was leading the Vuelta on August 29 and looked set to win the race for the first time. However he hit a large stone on the road approximately 33km from the finish, landing heavily and suffering those spinal injuries, a fractured collarbone and a concussion.

He tried to continue but was forced to withdraw from the race. He was brought to a local hospital and assessed, but then things took a surreal turn.

“I was just laying there and signing autographs for the doctors and nurses, taking some photos,” he told The Athletic.

“I was kind of out of it, and they were cutting my skin suit from the back, taking small pieces of the jersey, and asking if I could sign these parts of the skin suit. So my skin suit now has a lot of holes cut into it which I gave to the staff.”

Pogačar returned to Monaco several days later and was cared for by his partner, Urška Žigart . Things were initially very tough, with the Slovenian saying he struggled psychologically.

“For the first two weeks, I was really mentally not OK. I was really down. I was not a fun person to be around,” he stated.

“I don’t think Urška was happy to see me around the house, because I was just, like, depressed. You know, just not feeling anything.”

Things became more complicated two weeks after his return when Žigart crashed in the Faun Tour Femmes and reinjured the jaw she had fractured in the Tour de Suisse in June.

Fortunately Pogačar was starting to feel better by then and, over time, both of them were able to return to training.

Soon after his crash his team said that his season was over. In addition to missing out on the Vuelta win he was forced to abandon his bid to retain his world championship and European championship jerseys.

Still, as the Euros approached, there were rumours that he wanted to make a return. The championships were held in his native Slovenia and, as he noted, the road race was ten kilometers from his parents’ home.

He knew the roads extremely well and was motivated to return. However a follow up X-ray showed that his fracture was not healing quickly and with his team not keen for him to race, he backed off.

He subsequently found out that his T1 and T2 vertebrae were also fractured.

That poised additional risks, particularly if he fell again.

“Because it’s not as visible as a collarbone, everybody forgets about it, I think,” he said. “People who have experienced it, or know somebody that has broken vertebrae, knows how serious it is. It was strange because it was not really painful in the position where it was broken, I was focusing more on the collarbone.

“But if I crash again on the bike now, it can be very problematic. Everybody says that I was lucky, and you’re always lucky after a crash where you can walk away and you’re fine. But the more you talk with people, the more you find out about the seriousness of the injury. You have the internet and you google it. You see it’s pretty serious and not to joke around. It’s a bit scary, to be honest, to think about it.”

Pogačar is back training regularly, although caution about his injuries and the danger of another fall didn’t stop him from being accused of reckless riding in Monaco.

He will continue working hard and even if the Tour de France race director Christian Prudhomme suggested that he might not get back to his previous level, will aim to have a superb 2027.

If he does achieve that, fans will be relieved that the initial consequences of his crash were not as serious as could have been.

They’ll also be relieved that he didn’t line out in the Europeans unaware that he had not one but three spinal fractures.

The Tour de France threw a curveball at the peloton last week when it revealed its route for 2027.

The most time trial kilometers in 15 years. The fewest summit finishes in recent memory. Too many very long stages.

The route for the 2027 Tour de France is about as old-school as you can get, and one that’s already been labeled anti-Pogačar, pro-Remco, and designed to delight great French hope Paul Seixas.

But is Pogačar’s chance at a historic sixth yellow jersey really in peril?

And can we on the couch really count ourselves lucky that the Montmartre finale returns to stage 21 in Paris? We’ve got to sit through one of the most featureless parcours of the Pogi era to see the Tour’s monumental modern ending.

Here are some of the biggest winners and losers from the 2027 Tour de France course reveal.

The 2027 Tour de France has been called the “anti-Pog” Tour de France .

But there’s no such thing. You cannot Pogačar-proof Le Tour.

The controversial inclusion of 71km of flat time trialing won’t have Tadej Pogačar in a fluster as he plans his shot at a record-breaking sixth maillot jaune.

At the 2026 Tour de France, time trial topper Remco Evenepoel finished more than six minutes back on Pogačar. Assuming they both hold form into next July, Evenepoel will need to gain five seconds per kilometer to level with King Pog.

If you think that’s going to happen, I want some of what you’ve been smoking.

Jonas Vingegaard and Visma-Lease a Bike’s Killer Bees were stung by the Tour route presentation. The 2027 parcours does not suit the two-time winner, not one bit.

With just three high-summit finishes, next year’s race looks more like an “anti-Jonas” Tour than an “anti-Pog” Tour.

The course includes only one of the high-altitude, multi-mountain monster stages where Vingegaard typically thrives. The 18th “Queen Stage” in the Pyrénées is the only obvious place where the Scandi climbing goat might drop his punchier rivals.

Vingegaard can’t rely on making much time in the Alps and Pyrénées, and he’s not likely to take time on the TT bike, either.

The 29-year-old’s three-year wait to reclaim the yellow jersey might see a new anniversary next year in Paris.

Everybody except a handful of heavy sprinters won when ASO confirmed the showstopper Montmartre would return to stage 21 of the Tour de France.

After two breathless thrillers won by Wout van Aert and Mathieu van der Poel – two of the biggest names in world cycling – in 2025 and 2026, nobody wanted to see a return of the fusty old bunch sprint format in 2027.

Go block it out of your calendar right now.

ASO didn’t let us have it all our own way by putting Montmartre back on the parcours for 2027.

Next year’s Tour de France is one of the longest of the past decade.

Three stages nudge past 220km, three are close to 200km, and only the finale in Paris clocks in at under 150km.

Strip the two time trials from the total distance of 3,479km, and the remaining road stages average 179km in length. That’s too long.

What happened to the trend toward always-entertaining, super-digestible three-hour stages? Bite-sized packages of 120-160km seemed like the future for a sport struggling to find a new audience.

The weekend stages 8, 15, and 20 – the days where the couch, your snack supply, and the Tour de France are the only things that matter – are all set up as sprints or breakaways.

Oh, and that nothing-burger 20th stage? Don’t get us started.

Remco Evenepoel isn’t any more likely to beat Tadej Pogačar at the 2027 Tour de France than he was in the 2026 Tour de France. He’d need an act of god or some mid-90s “preparation” to make that happen.

But Red Bull’s “aero bullet” is without doubt in pole position for second on the podium.

Evenepoel hasn’t seen a route this favorable in his entire career. In fact, he was some teenage football player the last time the Tour de France was so clearly designed for a time trialist. “The Wiggins Tour” included a mind-numbing 101km against the clock in 2012.

Evenepoel should gain more than enough advantage over 71km of time trialing to offset any potential losses in the mountains. He further benefits from the lack of multi-mountain stages and high summit finishes that have proven his kryptonite in the past.

There had been rumor that Evenepoel will target a Giro-Tour double in 2027.

There’s surely no way he’s considering messing around with such a risky schedule now.

The Tour de France promo spiel suggests there are seven sprint stages on tap for 2027, but the peloton’s reigning sprint king ain’t so sure.

Tim Merlier has grumbled that heavyweights like himself and Jonathan Milan might see as few as four chances next year. And given the return of the Montmartre, there’s not even the lure of the Champs-Élysées.

Indeed, the 2027 route is tilted in favor of “modern,” versatile sprinters like Matthew Brennan or Merlier’s rising teammate, Paul Magnier. Accumulated climbing or late obstacles could cook the carthorses before they see some of the “sprint finishes” promised them in next year’s Tour de France.

The only consolation for the biggest, “purest” sprinters?

A strong chance at winning the first yellow jersey at the stage 1 grand départ into Carlisle.

The French nation breathed a collective sigh of relief last week when Christian Prudhomme released the route for the 2027 Tour de France.

The kid’s a monster on the time trial bike, and he’ll have plenty of opportunity to reinforce that fact next July. He also seems better on smaller, punchier climbs than towering high Alps. How convenient then, that there are relatively few of those.

Tour organizers ASO have a habit of weighting the Tour’s parcours in favor of its rider du jour .

And while we’re not suggesting that’s the case in 2027 – how dare we?! – there’s nothing on the parcours that might stop Seixas from bettering his debut fourth-place finish from 2026 next July.

But is that really a good thing for the 20-year-old?…

When the Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes revealed their new-look leaders’ jerseys last week, one color caught everybody’s eye.

The iconic white jersey of “best young rider,” last won by Isaac del Toro and Antonia Niedermaier, will get a facelift in 2027.

The typically pearly maillot has been embellished – or some may say, ruined – by an “ultraviolet” purple trim in a nod to the new jersey sponsor, Sanofi. The Paris-based biopharma company has made the lurid purple its “thing,” apparently.

The introduction of “ultraviolet” into the Tour de France palette has become a serious talking point in a cycling world without racing to argue about.

Purple bits are being debated with equal intensity to the 71km of time trialing in the men’s race and a crowning climb – the Puy de Dôme – at the Femmes that might be closed off to crowds.

“A hater has spent years infiltrating ASO and is now taking revenge by ruining one iconic jersey at a time,” is the brilliant title of one Reddit thread on the topic.

Calls of “fashion crimes,” “a Jayco away kit,” and vomit memes are doing the rounds on Twitter / X .

To be fair, not even the mustachioed model looks too impressed in the official marketing shot.

The Tour hasn’t seen this much confab over clothing since … since the last time race organizer ASO made everyone angry with its leader’s apparel.

In 2023, the vert points jersey turned from lime to forest green at the behest of jersey sponsor Škoda.

Couch Peloton has been in protest ever since.

The new maillot blan c of “best young rider” isn’t the only Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes leader’s jersey that will be relaunched next season.

Last week at the official route reveals , ASO revealed tweaked versions of all four of its iconic classification leaders’ jerseys.

The historic yellow, green, polka dot, and white tops have all gotten a refresh for 2027 courtesy of ASO’s new clothing supplier, Castelli.

The Italian brand returns to the Tour for the first time in more than 30 years in 2027. Santini had done the honors since 2022.

Castelli also takes charge of the sewing machine for the ASO-owned Paris-Roubaix, Paris-Nice, Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, and Vuelta a España.

The Tour de France jersey polemica is isolated to just the purple-on-white maillot blanc .

The maillots jaune , verte and à pois haven’t been messed with enough to catch public ire.

In a recent statement, Castelli brand manager Steve Smith paid tribute to the heft of the Tour’s classification jerseys.

“Producing the maillot jaune represents the highest possible honor. We wanted these jerseys to be truly special. That is why every micro-detail stems from our deep reverence for what they represent to the sport and the riders who earn them,” Smith said.

“Beyond pushing performance and aerodynamics, every single feature was crafted to honor that legacy.”

Some may argue purple is not a part of the Tour de France white jersey legacy.

Demi Vollering won the Tour de France Femmes for the second time this year (Photo: Tim de Waele/Getty Images) (Photo: Tim De Waele)

It lacks high altitude climbs but the route of next year’s Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift does something the men’s event doesn’t do.

The profiles of both races were unveiled Thursday in Paris by organizer ASO. Something that was immediately apparent was that the expected contest between Tadej Pogačar, Jonas Vingegaard, Remco Evenepoel, Paul Seixas and others runs the risk of fizzling out days before the conclusion in Paris.

This year stage 20 saw the riders duke it out to the summit of Alpe d’Huez, facing one of the Tour’s most notorious climbs on two successive days.

Pogačar was sufficiently far ahead by then to have the yellow jersey sewn up, but the battle for the podium still raged. Isaac del Toro ultimately distanced Seixas close to the finish and seal third overall.

Next summer? There is a danger of an anti-climax, with the last big mountain battle coming on stage 18’s summit finish at Saint Larry Soulan. The following stage does offer three climbs yet the highest of those, the Col de Soudet, is just 1540 meters above sea level and tops out 65km from the finish.

It is followed by the final categorized climb of the race, the Col de Marie Blanque. It’s a well-known peak, but while it is steep it is just 7.7km in duration and summits a full 18.5km from the finish line.

That’s not exactly a showdown, and the issue is compounded with a sprinters’ day out on stage 20 and a Montmartre-enhanced concluder in Paris which will offer good racing, but may well see the GC neutralized again.

All together, there is a danger the men’s Tour de France could end with a whimper, not a bang.

Fortunately, the same can’t be said of the Tour de France Femmes.

The Femmes race debuted in 2022 and has offered some of the best competition in pro cycling. Just consider the 2024 edition, which was every bit as much a cliffhanger as the conclusion of the men’s 1989 Tour.

Kasia Niewiadoma started the day in yellow, was dropped on the Col du Glandon, but fought all the way to the summit of Alpe d’Huez to win by just five seconds overall.

That was even closer than the classic 1989 showdown where Greg LeMond overhauled Laurent Fignon by eight seconds.

Last year’s race saw Pauline Ferrand Prétot stamp her authority all over the event, easily dropping her rivals in the mountains on the final two days. And while the Frenchwoman did have a 2:37 minute lead going into the final stage, the fact that it was a summit finish meant that there was—theoretically at least—the possibility that Vollering and others could turn things around.

The drama continued this summer when Vollering and Niewiadoma went into the hilly concluder in Nice a mere eight seconds apart.

It was, once again, a nailbiter, and left the outcome undecided right until the finale.

That kind of suspense will continue next summer, thanks to another well thought out route design. The race will again build steadily towards a crescendo, maintaining suspense in a way that the men’s Tour likely won’t.

In trying to avoid another Tadej Pogačar domination, the organizers have neutered things in a way that could backfire.

The Femmes course design avoids that problem. It’s not quite perfect, but it should be very entertaining.

As detailed by Velo’s Andy Hood this week, the Femmes route will begin in Leeds and offers three days of high-stakes racing on British soil. Day one heads to Manchester and takes in 85.7km of rolling terrain. Stage two crams nearly 3000 altitude meters of punchy racing into a 154.4km route to Sheffield, while stage three will be a tricky 18km team time trial in London.

That nervous start will be followed by three complicated transition stages on French soil, to Calais, Magnanville and Bourges respectively. Those offer something for the sprinters, but also for the attackers. Stage 5 in particular could be a puncheurs’ delight, with series of short, steep climbs in the final hour and a half of racing.

The GC battle really comes into focus on the final three stages. Stage 7 is almost completely flat for the first 100km but then concludes with a summit finish to the top of La Loge des Gardes. Sure, the final climb is just 6.7km but it is preceded by a tricky uphill approach which should see some very nervous racing.

Stage 8 is continuously up and down. It does lack a summit finish but 3000 meters of altitude gain en route to Clermont-Ferrand will lead to a lot of tension, particularly if time gaps are tight.

The big decider is stage nine’s summit finish to the top of the Puy de Dôme. The climb is an iconic one, most famous for a literal shoulder to shoulder battle between Jacques Anquetil and Raymond Poulidor in 1964.

Those slopes were closed to the Tour for many years but made a return to the men’s race in 2023, when Michael Woods won and Tadej Pogačar dropped Jonas Vingegaard, only to lose out overall.

It’s not as long or as tough as other iconic mountains in cycling but everything in the race builds towards this big showdown. And while fans were not allowed on the climb three years ago for the men’s Tour, there are suggestions this could change next summer.

It should be another gripping finale to the Tour de France Femmes, guaranteeing GC suspense right to the closing minutes. It’s something the men’s race should aspire to too yet, next year at least, almost certainly won’t.

That’s a shame for the men’s Tour. At least the Femmes will keep everyone guessing right until the end.

Can two time trials in the 2027 Tour de France be the key to victory for Remco Evenepoel? (Photo: Tim de Waele/Getty Images) (Photo: Tim De Waele)

Third in 2024, second this year. Is Remco Evenepoel heading towards victory in the 2027 Tour de France ?

His 6:26 deficit to Tadej Pogačar this time around suggests otherwise, but there are three factors which could narrow the gap considerably.

Firstly, there’s Pogačar’s big crash at the Vuelta a España. He suffered a concussion plus fractures to his neck and shoulder, and was forced to abandon the defense of his world and European championship titles.

While the Tour is still over eight months away, Tour de France race director Christian Prudhomme has suggested that fall might have a long-term effect on the five-time winner.

Correct or not, it’s clear his injuries and his curtailed season were less than ideal.

The second factor is the age gap between the two riders. Pogačar is now 28 and, if he follows the usual pattern seen with many athletes, he could see his performances start to plateau.

Evenepoel is a year and four months younger and, at 26, should continue to improve.

The third consideration is the gift the Tour de France organizers handed Evenepoel this week. Namely, the most time trial kilometers to feature in the race since 2012.

This year’s Tour had just 26.1 individual kilometers against the clock.

Next July will see more than double that, with the two TT’s totaling 71km.

That, plus the fact that there are just three summit finishes, two less than this season, means that Evenepoel will feel good about his chances.

While the Belgian was not at this week’s Tour presentation, his Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team gave a big thumbs up to the route.

Directeur sportif Zak Dempster referenced the two races against the clock and said those will help fight for the maillot jaune.

“The first week promises intense racing, where staying out of trouble will be key,” he said.

“The long ITT (individual time trial) at the end of that first week offers us a great opportunity to make an early statement right away. This could be crucial heading into the Alps in the second week.”

And while Evenepoel will then be up against Pogačar and the other favorites in the high mountains, he has a chance to gain further time in the other ITT.

“The second time trial is another highlight of this route,” Dempster continued.

“We welcome the return of more individual time trial kilometers, as this adds another dimension to the race and makes the battle for yellow even more open and exciting. Overall, it’s a route that plays to our strengths and gives us every reason to aim for yellow.”

As for team CEO Ralph Denk, he too was upbeat.

“Remco is the best time triallist at the moment, world champion, and definitely he would be happy. We have two time trials here, more than 70k in TT,” he told VTM Nieuws .

However Denk played down suggestions that three rather than five mountain-top finishes made it an easier Tour in terms of climbing.

“I see this a bit differently because we have a stage of more than 5000 climbing meters,” he said. “It is a super tough one. And there are other climbs here. Let’s see. Let’s evaluate in detail. I will not confirm this is an easy Tour de France.”

“It is always the goal from our team to battle to the best, and let’s see. But for this answer, we need to have a closer look at the route.”

Evenepoel completed the season with a fine statistic. He rode five individual time trials this season, and he won each of them.

He took the TT at the Tour and also won his fourth world championship title, then defended his European champs crown.

He ended off the year with a resounding victory in the Chrono des Nations TT. Evenepoel finished a staggering 2:11 ahead of Jay Vine (UAE Emirates-XRG) there, and said afterwards that everything came together perfectly.

“The handling, the speed and the feeling of being one with the bike all felt really good. Looking ahead to next year, it was all very promising,” he stated.

That kind of performance is why former professional Jan Bakelandts is predicting huge gains in the Tour.

“Remco is genuinely the best time triallist in the world,” he stated in his HLN.be column . “I wouldn’t rule out him taking two minutes out of Pogačar across those two time trials, provided he can reproduce the level he showed at the world championships.

“That’s crucial: he’ll have to be just as brilliant as he was in Montreal, because Pogačar’s track record in the Tour is also astonishingly strong.”

It’s a valid point. Despite Evenepoel’s far greater pedigree as a TT rider, Pogačar limited his losses to 28 seconds in the Tour’s individual time trial this year.

That was over a distance of 26.1km, meaning he gave up just over one second per kilometer.

If he puts in the same kind of performances across the two TTs next summer he will surrender around one minute 11 seconds.

But others such as five time Tour de France winner Bernard Hinault aren’t so sure.

“This Tour is still too hard for him,” he told Nieuwsblad . “This year he has made a nice progression. He had a lower weight and climbed a lot better. But sharp attacks uphill he does not tolerate. Evenepoel is a steady climber. I think he can win stages next year, especially the two time trials.

“But I don’t believe in the general classification. There’s just one that’s better than the rest. And Pogačar will want revenge for the Vuelta.”

Still, Hinault is aware that nothing is guaranteed in sport. He knows pro cycling very well, but also understands that surprises can happen.

“I could be wrong,” he accepted. “And Evenepoel himself must think that he can make it.”

That possibility will sustain the Belgian over the winter months, giving him focus and additional self-belief as he builds towards 2027 and his best Tour prospects thus far.

Demi Vollering just wrapped up the greatest season in the pro peloton.

The Dutchwoman obliterated the women’s UCI rankings with a season-long rout that won her the Giro d’Italia, Tour de France, road world championships, and a whole lot more.

Vollering topped the 2026 year-end rankings with a haul of 9,330 UCI points – some 65 percent more than second-place Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney. Vollering’s Polish nemesis finished the year on 5,660 points.

Spanish super talent Paula Blasi rounded out her breakout season third in the rankings with 5,201 points.

Vollering’s season wasn’t only the best in the women’s road peloton.

It was more impressive than anything achieved on the men’s side of the sport, too.

This year, Vollering strung together a 2026 season even more dominant than Tadej Pogačar’s.

Yes, the Slovenian won the Tour de France for a record-breaking fifth time, unlocked Milan-San Remo, and topped the UCI league by echelons, despite racing for only six months.

He probably would have also won the Vuelta, worlds, and Il Lombardia if a brutal crash didn’t prematurely end his season.

Vollering won two monuments, the world and European titles, and topped the GC of every stage-race she started.

The 29-year-old became only the second woman after Annemiek van Vleuten to complete the triple crown.

And she hit the podium of every one-day road race she started bar Strade Bianche. Being directed off course (depending on your reading of the situation) at the sterrato classic will do that to one’s podium aspirations, we guess.

Vollering’s 2026 season was a masterpiece on-par with anything that GOATs like Van Vleuten, Anna van der Breggen, or Marianne Vos have put together. It was a Hall of Fame eight months that saw FDJ Suez’s superstar leader amass more UCI points than eight women’s WorldTour teams.

Dem Vollering: Rider of the year. Gotta be .

The 2026 UCI rider and team rankings, and a ranking of rider victories, can be found at the bottom of this post.

Here is our breakdown and hot takes from the 2026 men’s rankings.

One thing Vollering didn’t do this year?

But we’ll let her off. Super-mega sprinter Lorena Wiebes was in her own orbit , again.

With a total of 24 victories, Wiebes won the most for the third year in a row. Not even a controversial bike weight disqualification at the Giro d’Italia slowed the 27-year-old’s High Speed Express.

Vollering ranked second in individual wins with 16.

The extent of Wiebes’ and Vollering’s dominance over the Women’s WorldTour is brutally clear if you scan further down the year end victory table.

With “only” 8 and 7 wins apiece, some might think Marlen Reusser and Blasi in third and fourth were riding with brake rub.

Picnic-PostNL’s troubles are not isolated to the men’s peloton.

The under-scrutiny Dutch team is dead-last in the Women’s WorldTour rankings with a total of 2,450 points. That’s 11 percent of the most successful team, UAE L’Imad. The news that long-time leader Pfeiffer Georgi is headed for the exit door will compound Picnic-PostNL’s problems in 2027.

Speaking of UAE l’Imad – the Women’s WorldTour got a new superteam in 2026.

The UAE-based squad topped the UCI charts for the first time courtesy of its prolific leadership trident Blasi, Elisa Longo Borghini, and Dominika Wlodarczyk.

Former dominators FDJ United-Suez and SD Worx-ProTime went two-three, respectively.

But getting to the top ain’t the same as staying at the top.

UAE L’Imad’s winning season might be a one-and-done. Blasi’s blockbuster move to Movistar will blow a hole in her former UAE team in 2027.

Last up – take a look at the rankings again.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot has bombed out of the top 20 after her incredible 2025 season. PFP was woman of the year in 2025 after she won both Paris-Roubaix and the Tour de France femmes.

This year, the template that had worked so well for the Frenchwoman went very wrong, and her form nosedived soon after spring.

Ferrand-Prévot’s year-end ranking of 31st says a lot about her annus horribilis.

But it might not paint the fairest picture.

PFP wasn’t near the top of the board in 2025, either. The 34-year-old races so selectively that she finished only 13th in 2025.

Ferrand-Prévot doesn’t care about points, she cares about history and legacy. 2026 was no doubt a season she’ll be hoping gets lost in the mists of time.

Cyclists who are sick of the frightening cost and ghastly gloop of energy gels should consider dressing as a demon and going trick-or-treating this Halloween.

The candy that will be dished out to expectant ghouls and gremlins this weekend is almost perfect riding fuel.

Kids’ favorites like Nerds Gummy Clusters, Sour Patch Kids, and the ever-controversial candy corn can deliver 10 times more energy per dollar and multiple times more flavor per mouthful than primo sports nutrition products.

But before you go craft a costume and muster a trick-or-treat patrol, there are a few things you should know.

They might save your candy-fueled bike rides from becoming a fright.

Carbs are the body’s preferred source of fast energy , but they’re a limited resource. The muscles and liver can only store a limited amount of carbohydrates, making it essential to top up during any longer, harder ride. Those who don’t face the prospect of an empty fuel tank and a miserable slog home.

Halloween candy provides exactly what the working muscles need: fast-acting, low-fiber carbohydrates.

At the basic level, it’s no different from the gels and drinks that promise to bonk-proof your ride with perfectly synthesized packages of energy.

And we all know the promise of sport nutrition comes at a price. A packet of “pina colada” or “birthday cake” flavor sports goo can cost close to five bucks.

When we compared the cost and nutritional values of nine popular Halloween candies to some of our favored gels, the results were not surprising.

A couple of handfuls of candy will deliver the same amount of carbohydrate as a leading energy gel, at just a fraction of the price.

For example, per our calculations, every gram of carbohydrate in a hyper-researched Maurten hydrogel costs 11 cents. One gram of carbohydrate from the Halloween love-or-hate candy corn costs one cent.

So that’s it, right? No energy gels, ever again?

Not all carbs are created equal, and candy carbs are not always the best carbs for workout fuel – no matter how damn cheap and tasty they might be.

The modern sports nutrition that enabled the high-carb fueling “revolution ” uses specific sugar blends to maximize carbohydrate absorption into the gut and oxidation by the muscles.

By using both glucose and fructose in 1:0.8 or 2:1 ratios, leading products allow athletes like Tadej Pogačar to fuel at more than 500 calories of carbs per hour, for six hours straight.

Try that with a bag of Twizzlers; we dare you. Maybe stash some toilet paper in your jersey pocket if you do.

Mass-market candy rarely, if ever, uses the glucose-to-fructose ratios that have saved the WorldTour from the explosive G.I. distress that once haunted high-carb fueling. Targeting the pro-standard 120 grams of carbs per hour with a packet of Sour Patch Kids will result in scenes worthy of the most icky horror movie.

If you hope to “train hard” rather than just “ride,” skip the sweeties. Invest in your workout and splurge on sports nutrition.

In many cases, energy gels and drinks are not just energy.

Many products are boosted with stimulants like caffeine or taurine, or minerals like sodium and potassium.

Electrolyte supplementation can be especially important for any rider going long or going hard. Candy won’t help keep sodium balance in check.

By contrast, candies can include things you might not want in the fueling mix.

Fiber and fats are not your friends if you need fast energy. They slow digestion, and can cause gut rot if eaten during workout intensity.

So, we’re sorry to say it, Snickers fans. That delicious stick of chocolate and nuts might wreck your workout. Save it for when you get home – your stomach will thank you, and your jersey lining might, too. There’s no coming back from finding a melted chocolate bar smooshed into your back pocket after a long or hot ride.

If you want fast fuel, choose your Halloween candy carefully. Nerds Gummy Clusters, Sour Patch Kids, and Skittles will give you more speed than Snickers or Reese’s.

But that’s not to say chocolate doesn’t have a place in your cycling cupboard.

For long, low-intensity rides, chocolate’s satiety and slower-release energy can see you right for endless kilometers. Just ask Oreo and Payday bar afficionado , Lachlan Morton.

But for the sake of your sleek new apparel, consider how you carry it.

And perhaps two of the most obvious considerations when considering gels vs. candy: Portability and munch-ability.

As tasty as Nerds Gummy Clusters might be, anyone who’s tried chewing them down mid-effort is in for a fright. The choking hazard of small candies is very real if you’re trying to hit a workout.

And that’s if you can even access them while on the move.

An easily overlooked benefit of an energy gel is just how easy it is to access and open while you’re clinging to the wheels of the weekend group ride. Ever tried tearing open a packet of Sour Patch Kids with frozen mid-winter fingers while riding 350 watts? Trust us, don’t bother.

A couple of real-food fueling transportation tips?

Pre-open candy packets before you go ride for easy accessibility.

And if you can’t face a six-hour ride without a Twix, we get it. But stash it in the bar bag, not the pocket of your $150 jersey.

Considering some over-age trick-or-treating this weekend?

Here’s how Team Velo ’s favorite candies compare to some leading energy gels to help guide your Halloween ghouling.

We’ve included the costs and total nutritional values of packet sizes often found in a local store, and added our golden metric: cost per carbohydrate.

We’ve also included some reasonable serving sizes for cyclists meticulous enough to split an XL sack of sweets into portions before they ride.

Candy can give you 10 times more carbs per dollar than sport nutrition.

Candy corn worked out as the cheapest of all the grocery store treats, but could you handle the polarizing, waxy consistency?…

"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.

"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.

"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.

He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".

"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.

A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.

In April, Google said people are now translating , external one trillion words a month with Google Translate.

That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.

Direct sales of machine translation , external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.

"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.

Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.

"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.

But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.

"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.

Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.

She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.

"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.

The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.

When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".

In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.

The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.

Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.

"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.

She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).

"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.

She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.

Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.

Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".

Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.

Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.

"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.…

Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois.

The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma.

The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found.

For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator.

The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US.

Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases.

The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer.

They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms.

Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual.

Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the killer's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member.

"That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime.

It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year.

Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this."

The technique that led detectives to Zigler is credited with revolutionising how forensic cases are solved.

It has been highly successful in helping solve cases involving unidentified human remains and identifying suspects in longstanding investigations.

Othram claims it has helped solve thousands of cases. The company's chief executive David Mittelman likens investigative genetic genealogy to a GPS system: "The DNA profile is the GPS signal and it says 'you belong here.' But to understand where 'here' is, you need a map."

Public records, obituaries, and census data build that map so Othram's scientists can establish how different family trees connect.

However, Mittelman is quick to point out that DNA technology can only go so far before "a cascade of investigative steps" are needed.

DNA science isn't the only technology that are helping detectives solve cold cases.

One of the challenges facing detectives on major cases investigations like the hunt for Sperino's killer is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up.

Officers investigating Sperino's murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993.

They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case.

The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot.

This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence.

But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them."

Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique."

"But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds.

While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data.

"There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London. While one person may have opted in to their DNA being used, genetic relatives may not have given consent.

A lack of funding is another hurdle. Mittelman says: "Every law enforcement agency wants to do it. There's just not a lot of funding for it."

Sometimes cases are funded through donations or crowdfunding. Othram operates a website listing cases that members of the public can help fund.

While investigative genetic genealogy has been adopted in countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Australia, it is not yet used in the UK. The Home Office is conducting a study to consider whether it should be adopted in the UK but did not respond to a request for comment.

The UK is already in a strong position, says Syndercombe Court. "We have such an efficient DNA database that if you can get any DNA out of a crime scene, you've got over a 65% chance of putting a name to that person, which is enormously powerful," she says.

On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".

Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external

Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external

With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.

As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.

Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.

In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.

The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.

Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America

Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.

Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."

Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.

So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.

On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.

Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.

Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.

He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."

And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.

Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year.

Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.

The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.

Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.

From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.

Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.

Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.

Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.

Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.

This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.

"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.

The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.

That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.

"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.

If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.

While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.…

Chancellor John Healey has announced his Budget, which includes changes to minimum wage and help for people trying to get onto the housing ladder.

Here is how the Budget could affect you if you are under-25.

If you are an 18-to-20 year-old earning the minimum wage, your pay will go up by 3.9% from next April.

However, the increase may be lower than you had expected. That is because Healey reversed course on how his Labour predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had been increasing the minimum wage for young people.

Labour had promised to do away with "discriminatory age bands", with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage. This year, 18-20 year-olds will see the same increase as older workers, meaning the disparity will remain. So, for 18-to-20 year-olds, your pay will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.

The increase also means a 21-year-old, who is working full time on the minimum wage and took out a student loan after 2023, will now earn enough to meet the £25,000 repayment threshold, over which they will start paying back 9% of their earnings.

The Budget contained plans to help people get onto the housing ladder, including the introduction of a "First Time Buyer Isa". This is an account in which savers can build up a deposit, with the government topping up contributions of up to £4,000 each year with a 25% bonus.

The new savings account will be introduced in 2029, replacing the existing Lifetime Isa, which has been criticised by some for imposing harsh penalties on those buying homes for more than the £450,000 cap.

The cap will remain, but the new "First Time Buyer Isa" will ensure savers are not penalised by losing their own money when making withdrawals. Savers will only lose contributions made by the government when making withdrawals which are not eligible for the account.

The penalty for withdrawals from existing Lifetime Isas will be lowered, too, to address concerns about savers being punished.

The government had already revealed a £4.7bn scheme for first-time buyers in England dubbed Your First Home. It is aiming to help 70,000 individuals and couples get on the housing ladder

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It will provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

Capped at £110,000 outside London and £140,000 in the capital, it is aimed at those hoping to get on the housing ladder without help from "the bank of mum and dad".

If you are a young person hoping to start a business in England, the Budget contained good news for you.

The chancellor wants to level the playing field for young entrepreneurs who have bright ideas, but who might not have the same family financial backing as others.

In an attempt to encourage more young people to start their own businesses, the government will pilot a "Young Entrepreneurs Allowance" in England.

The allowance will see your living costs partly covered by the government for the first year your business is operating. Healey hopes it will encourage more young people to take the plunge and become entrepreneurs.

Details of the scheme are thin at the moment, however, only that it will be rolled out "shortly".

On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall.

Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered San Francisco start-up Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology.

The company claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours.

This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below.

Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska.

Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat.

"It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says.

Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation."

Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished , external ", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers , external in more than three decades.

Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles.

Nevertheless, more than 50 countries , external are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain.

As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it.

Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times.

He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable."

Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation.

Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flairs, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain.

Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region."

Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas.

While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground.

"With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center.

What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges.

In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry. "Drones [such as Rainmaker's products] present this new avenue," says Meyer, "and they offer a more targeted nature to these clouds we hope will be responsive."

What is sprayed into clouds may also be undergoing a major shift. Recast Systems in San Francisco is experimenting with a type of protein made from amino acids found in the soil, says CEO Olivia Li.

While still undergoing tests at Texas A&M University, this new seeding agent moves Recast away from silver iodide as the go-to compound.

"It's safe, biodegradable and nucleates ice at a higher efficiency than silver iodide," says Li, whose company currently uses silver iodide to seed clouds in several US states.

Meyer is optimistic this technology's trajectory will only continue to rise. "We're going to see more demand for these services as so many regions are experiencing water demand," he says, "and they're going to be looking for ways to help bridge that gap."

People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.

Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.

Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.

The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.

In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a £100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.

But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.

"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.

"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.

However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.

Treasury will not commit to reducing welfare bill before next election

What we now know about the UK economy in four charts

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

In response the government had provided a "scattergun" Budget that did not do enough to address the challenges facing the country, Curtice said.

Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" £600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains made in the first five years.

Even after the extra support provided by the government, households will be left paying higher energy bills than during the last energy crisis in 2022, according to its analysis.

The Resolution Foundation said the support should have been more targeted at the poorest households.

Alongside the Budget the OBR issued its economic forecast indicating a slowdown in GDP growth from 1.2% in 2026 to 1% in 2027.

The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March.

The OBR also put its forecast for inflation for 2027 up from 2% to 3.4%.

Frozen tax thresholds are also eating into people's take-home pay.

However, the OBR also emphasised the difficulties in economic forecasting, highlighting uncertainty over the future path of inflation, in particular, which could turn out to be either significantly higher or lower than their predictions.

While the Resolution Foundation focused its forecast for living standards on working age households, the OBR looks at all households, including pensioners and reflects a 10-year rolling average growth to take into account short-term fluctuations.

The OBR found that by the end of the decade living standards for all households would have barely grown, by less than 0.1% per year.

"This decade looks set to be the worst decade for growth in household incomes on record," added the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS).

"No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy."

IFS director Helen Miller said there would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament.

"Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said.

"Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added.

Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions.

Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could.

He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households.

Around 20 million households are set to receive the £100 payment based on which council tax band they are in.

But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" of the amount of buffer the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends.

Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the £100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.

The UK may have no involvement in the US-Iran war, but the country is feeling the full force of the conflict on its economy.

Soaring energy prices are set to dent growth in the short term, push up inflation and leave living standards in a "grim" place, according to the latest official forecast from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Interest rates are also predicted to rise, making borrowing more expensive, along with government debt repayments.

Chancellor John Healey warned the nation faces "real challenges ahead" as he announced policies that he said would offer "breathing space" for households in the coming months.

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

"What we face today are global economic storms," he said. "We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them."

In its first assessment of the UK economy since the Middle East conflict started, the OBR said rising energy prices were the biggest risk to the economy in the near future.

Despite raising its growth forecast for this year, it sharply cut its prediction for next year from 1.6% to 1%.

Growth is then set to rebound in the following years.

When an economy grows, businesses tend to invest more, create more jobs and give pay rises to workers, which leaves people feeling better off on average, though it can take time and not everyone necessarily benefits.

Companies making higher profits also pay more in tax, which can enable the government to spend more on public services. When there is slow economic growth, or the economy shrinks, the opposite can occur.

Inflation can weigh on growth and the OBR has forecast that prices are set to rise at a faster pace as higher energy bills filter through supply chains and to consumers, especially in 2027.

High global oil prices have already hit drivers at the pumps, with petrol priced at almost £1.73 per litre on average, while diesel is near £1.99.

Elevated oil prices over time can lead to prices edging upwards across a host of goods, such as food, as companies pass on the higher expenses they face to consumers.

Goods are typically transported to destinations by lorries and vans, so high fuel prices can have far-reaching consequences.

The OBR now thinks inflation will stay higher for longer than previously forecast, peaking at 3.8% in 2027.

Despite the cost-of-living support announced by the government, economists at Pantheon Macroeconomics said the measures were "small beer given the surge in inflation we expect over the winter".

High inflation paints a bleak picture when it comes to living standards and the OBR has forecast a dip next year as energy bills hit the spending power of households.

Those on lower incomes are set to be hit harder, however, because energy costs eat up a bigger share of their monthly budget and disposable income.

Real household disposable income, a measure of living standards, is forecast to grow from 2027, but not by as much as previously thought.

"It's a pretty grim picture," according to the OBR's David Miles, who says there has been "virtually no growth" for individuals since before the Covid pandemic.

"It's been a dismal period in British economic history."

What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out

Inflation is expected to average 3.4% next year, before falling to the Bank of England's 2% target towards the end of the decade.

The Bank is widely expected to raise interest rates next week due to higher inflation in recent months. Rates are currently at 3.75%, but the OBR now forecasts they could rise to as high as 4.5% in the coming years.

It had previously forecast two interest rate cuts this year.

Higher rates makes borrowing money more expensive but can boost returns on savings.

Inflation also raises the cost of borrowing for the government, with spending on debt interest set to rise.

Such repayments are also predicted to increase the overall amount the government borrows, which is set to increase every year by more than had been previously forecast by the OBR.

Higher spending on welfare and pensions due to inflation is also expected to increase borrowing, though it is forecast to fall as a share of the economy over the next five years.

However, forecasts are only a best guess at what might happen in the future. Given the way the conflict in the Middle East has upended previous predictions, the future of the war could alter inflation expectations.

US President Donald Trump has suggested the war will end after the mid-term elections next month.

The OBR admitted there remained "significant uncertainty" around its predictions due to the changing situation in the Middle East.
